checkpoint.prompt: Is the second good-draw probability still 5/8 after a good first draw without replacement?
checkpoint.explanation: One good object has already been removed; the second probability is 4/7.

title: Two-way probability tables and independence
summary: Contingency tables summarize joint, marginal and conditional frequencies. Two events are independent precisely when P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B) for events with well-defined probabilities.
concept: Contingency tables summarize joint, marginal and conditional frequencies. Two events are independent precisely when P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B) for events with well-defined probabilities.
method: Sum all cells to obtain N. Divide cells and margins by N; compute P(A|B) using the relevant B margin, and compare with P(A) only after checking P(B)>0.
guardrail: An observed frequency table gives empirical probabilities; sampling variation means approximate equality is not automatic proof of population independence. Distinguish mutually exclusive from independent events.
reference: Morin, Probability for the Enthusiastic Beginner, foundational chapters; Lipschutz, Schaum Probability; Navidi, 4th ed., Ch. 2

workedExample.prompt: Among 200 boards, 30 have both defect A and condition B; 75 have condition B. Estimate P(A|B).
steps: Conditional denominator is the 75 boards with B.

checkpoint.prompt: For two events of positive probability, does mutual exclusivity imply independence?
checkpoint.explanation: Mutual exclusivity makes their intersection probability zero, while independence would require the positive product P(A)P(B).

title: Geometric distribution and first-success waiting time
summary: The geometric distribution counts independent Bernoulli trials up to and including the first success. With constant success probability p, P(X=k)=(1−p)^(k−1)p and E(X)=1/p.
concept: The geometric distribution counts independent Bernoulli trials up to and including the first success. With constant success probability p, P(X=k)=(1−p)^(k−1)p and E(X)=1/p.
method: Check independent identical trials, fixed p and first-success support k=1,2,... . Compute the required failures before the first success and apply the pmf.
guardrail: Some references define a geometric variable as failures before first success, which shifts the support and mean. Always state the chosen convention.
reference: Montgomery & Runger, 3rd ed., Chs. 3–5; Walpole et al., 9th ed., Chs. 3–6; Navidi, 4th ed., Ch. 4

workedExample.prompt: A test succeeds independently with probability 0.20. What is the expected number of trials until first success?

checkpoint.prompt: Does the trial-count geometric distribution include X=0?
checkpoint.explanation: With X defined as number of trials through the first success, the support starts at 1.

title: Hypergeometric sampling versus binomial trials
summary: Hypergeometric probabilities describe the successes in a fixed-size sample drawn without replacement from a finite population. Binomial probabilities describe a fixed number of independent Bernoulli trials with constant success rate.
concept: Hypergeometric probabilities describe the successes in a fixed-size sample drawn without replacement from a finite population. Binomial probabilities describe a fixed number of independent Bernoulli trials with constant success rate.
method: Identify the finite population size N, number K of successes and sample size n. Count the ways to choose k successes and n−k failures, then divide by C(N,n).
guardrail: Do not apply a binomial model blindly to substantial without-replacement sampling when dependence matters. Hypergeometric supports only feasible success counts.
reference: Montgomery & Runger, 3rd ed., Chs. 3–5; Walpole et al., 9th ed., Chs. 3–6; Navidi, 4th ed., Ch. 4

workedExample.prompt: A batch has 6 acceptable and 4 defective units. Two units are drawn without replacement. Find probability both are defective.

checkpoint.prompt: Is sampling repeatedly from a small finite lot without replacement exactly binomial?
checkpoint.explanation: The draws become dependent and success probability changes; use a hypergeometric model.

title: Exponential lifetimes and constant hazard models
summary: The exponential distribution models nonnegative waiting times under a constant event rate λ. Its survival probability is exp(−λt), its cumulative distribution is 1−exp(−λt), and its mean is 1/λ.
concept: The exponential distribution models nonnegative waiting times under a constant event rate λ. Its survival probability is exp(−λt), its cumulative distribution is 1−exp(−λt), and its mean is 1/λ.
method: Confirm that a constant-hazard waiting-time model is appropriate. Convert the rate into the reciprocal of the time units, then evaluate survival or cumulative failure probability at the desired time.
guardrail: Constant hazard is a substantive model assumption and may fail for aging or wear-out components. The memoryless property is specific to the exponential waiting-time model.
reference: Montgomery & Runger, 3rd ed., Chs. 3–5; Walpole et al., 9th ed., Chs. 3–6; Navidi, 4th ed., Ch. 4

workedExample.prompt: An exponential lifetime has λ=0.5 failures/hour. Compute mean lifetime.
steps: For exponential rate λ=0.5 per hour, E(T)=1/λ.

checkpoint.prompt: Does constant-hazard exponential modeling automatically describe devices whose failure rate rises with age?
checkpoint.explanation: Age-dependent wear-out behavior violates the exponential constant-hazard assumption.

title: Cumulative distribution functions and percentiles
summary: A cumulative distribution function F(x)=P(X≤x) describes the probability at or below a threshold. For discrete variables, jumps encode probability masses; for continuous variables, density integrates to cumulative probability.
concept: A cumulative distribution function F(x)=P(X≤x) describes the probability at or below a threshold. For discrete variables, jumps encode probability masses; for continuous variables, density integrates to cumulative probability.
method: Use F(b)−F(a) to compute interval probability P(a<X≤b). For discrete endpoints use care with strict versus non-strict inequalities and any point probability at a.
guardrail: A continuous density is not itself a probability at a point. Do not use F(b)−F(a) for an interval with a different endpoint convention without adjusting discrete masses.
reference: Montgomery & Runger, 3rd ed., Chs. 3–5; Walpole et al., 9th ed., Chs. 3–6; Navidi, 4th ed., Ch. 4

workedExample.prompt: A variable has F(2)=0.25 and F(5)=0.85. Find P(2<X≤5).

checkpoint.prompt: For a discrete distribution, does P(X=a) have to be zero?
checkpoint.explanation: A jump of the CDF at a may be positive and equals P(X=a).

title: Joint variables, covariance and linear combinations
summary: Joint distributions describe two random variables simultaneously. Expectations are linear without independence, while the variance of a sum additionally includes twice the covariance term.
concept: Joint distributions describe two random variables simultaneously. Expectations are linear without independence, while the variance of a sum additionally includes twice the covariance term.
method: Calculate each mean, variance and covariance from a valid joint distribution. For aX+bY, use expected value aE(X)+bE(Y) and variance a²Var(X)+b²Var(Y)+2abCov(X,Y).
guardrail: Independence implies zero covariance when the moments exist, but zero covariance does not generally imply independence. Dropping the covariance term requires justification.
reference: Montgomery & Runger, 3rd ed., Chs. 3–5; Walpole et al., 9th ed., Chs. 3–6; Navidi, 4th ed., Ch. 4

workedExample.prompt: Independent errors X and Y have variances 4 and 9. What is variance of X+Y?

checkpoint.prompt: When two measurements share noise sources, may we assume their covariance is zero?
checkpoint.explanation: Common measurement noise can induce dependence and nonzero covariance; assess its contribution.

title: Normal approximation and continuity correction
summary: For sufficiently large binomial counts away from extreme probabilities, a normal approximation may be used. Its mean is np and variance np(1−p), and continuity correction maps integer bounds to neighboring half-integer limits.
concept: For sufficiently large binomial counts away from extreme probabilities, a normal approximation may be used. Its mean is np and variance np(1−p), and continuity correction maps integer bounds to neighboring half-integer limits.
method: Check np and n(1−p) and choose an appropriate approximation accuracy. For P(X≤k), approximate using normal P(Y≤k+0.5), standardizing with mean np and sd sqrt(np(1−p)). A common classroom screening rule is both np≥5 and n(1−p)≥5 (some references recommend 10); check the desired accuracy and use the exact binomial distribution when either count is small. For P(X≥k), use normal cutoff k−0.5; for P(X≤k), use k+0.5.
guardrail: Approximation adequacy depends on n and p; extreme probabilities or small expected counts may demand an exact binomial calculation. Clearly state when a continuity correction is used. If the binomial is highly skewed (p near 0 or 1), the approximation may be poor even when n appears large; do not treat the threshold rule as a proof of accuracy.
reference: Montgomery & Runger, 3rd ed., Chs. 3–5; Walpole et al., 9th ed., Chs. 3–6; Navidi, 4th ed., Ch. 4

workedExample.prompt: For X~Binomial(100,0.5), give corrected z-boundary for P(X≤54).

checkpoint.prompt: Should P(X≤54) use 54.5 rather than 54 as the continuity-corrected normal cutoff?
checkpoint.explanation: The continuous approximation to count X≤54 uses an upper boundary at 54.5.
